claims.text: Resistance of HEAs to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the dynamic formation and self-healing of a mechanically robust passivating surface film.
Selective oxidation of corrosion-resistant alloying elements at freshly exposed wear surfaces produces the protective film.
The passivating film protects the alloy during concurrent mechanical abrasion and chemical attack.
Cr, Al, and Ni are examples of alloying elements capable of forming stable, protective oxides in the proposed HEA.
Oxidizing conditions must be maintained during tribocorrosion to permit passive-film formation.
Mechanical abrasion continuously renews the surface and exposes fresh alloy.
In an oxygen-containing corrosive medium, specific alloying elements oxidize preferentially to form a thin, adherent, self-healing oxide film.
The regenerated oxide film acts as a barrier to both further mechanical damage and chemical dissolution.
Dynamic regeneration of the film reduces overall degradation under combined wear-corrosion conditions.
A film-forming HEA will show lower combined material loss, shallower wear tracks, and lower corrosion rates than a matched alloy lacking selective surface enrichment.
The film-forming HEA will perform better during tribocorrosion than under the wear-only or corrosion-only baselines.
Suppressing passive-film formation will result in higher simultaneous wear and corrosion rates.
The predicted protection holds when sufficient oxygen or other oxidizing species are available and the mechanical load remains below the film's self-repair capacity.
The protective mechanism may fail in extremely anoxic environments or under loads high enough to prevent film reformation.
Reducing or substituting key film-forming elements provides a controlled means of testing the proposed mechanism against the full-composition HEA.
Statistically similar degradation rates and surface characteristics in the full-composition and modified samples would falsify the proposed film-mediated advantage.
